options.1: This swaps the two events round. $\P(A \mid B)$ and $\P(B \mid A)$ are different numbers, and Bayes' theorem is precisely the statement of how far apart they can be — it needs the two base rates, which you were not given.
options.2: This drops the condition entirely. You were told something about licence-holders only; the people without licences could own cars at any rate at all, and nothing here constrains them.
options.3: This confuses a conditional with a joint probability. $\P(A \cap B) = \P(A \mid B)\,\P(B)$, so it would be $0.8$ only if everyone had a licence.

feedback.reconsider: For each option, ask: which population is it talking about? The given number is about licence-holders. Only one option stays inside that population.

distractors.0: Correct. For a fixed condition, probabilities of complementary events add to $1$: $\P(A^c \mid B) = 1 - \P(A \mid B)$. Conditioning on $B$ is an ordinary probability measure on $B$.
distractors.1: No. This is the inverted conditional, and Bayes shows it depends on $\P(\text{licence})$ and $\P(\text{car})$, neither of which was given.
distractors.2: No. Nothing was said about people without licences, so the unconditional rate is not determined.
distractors.3: No. $\P(A \cap B) = \P(A \mid B)\P(B) = 0.8 \times \P(\text{licence})$, which is $0.8$ only if $\P(\text{licence}) = 1$.

explanation:
## The one that holds

Fix the condition $B$. Then $\P(\cdot \mid B)$ is itself a probability measure — it satisfies all the usual rules — so

$$\P(A^c \mid B) = 1 - \P(A \mid B) = 0.2.$$

Complements work **on the left of the bar**, as long as the right-hand side does not move.

## The three that do not

**Swapping the bar.** $\P(A \mid B) \ne \P(B \mid A)$ in general, and Bayes says exactly how they relate:

$$\P(B \mid A) = \P(A \mid B)\,\frac{\P(B)}{\P(A)}.$$

The ratio of base rates can be anything, so the two conditionals can be arbitrarily far apart. Nearly every famous probability error in medicine and in law is this swap.

**Dropping the condition.** The law of total probability gives

$$\P(A) = \P(A \mid B)\P(B) + \P(A \mid B^c)\P(B^c),$$

and the second term is entirely unconstrained here.

**Conditional versus joint.** $\P(A \cap B) = \P(A \mid B)\P(B)$, which is at most $\P(B)$ — a joint probability can never exceed either of its parts.

## The habit that prevents all three

Read $\P(A \mid B)$ out loud as *"among the $B$s, the proportion that are $A$"*. Then each wrong option becomes obviously about a different group of people: option 2 is about car owners, option 3 about everybody, option 4 about everybody again.
